Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always have the same value. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each addition usually produces an exact intermediate result that must be rounded to the nearest representable number. Changing the grouping changes which intermediate values are rounded, so it can change the final result.

For example, suppose a is a very large positive number, b is the corresponding large negative number, and c is comparatively small. Computing a + b first may produce zero, after which adding c returns c. Computing b + c first may cause c to be lost because it is too small to affect b at the available precision. Adding a afterward may then return zero. Both results follow the floating-point rules, even though they differ.

This behavior is fundamental to formats such as IEEE 754 binary32 and binary64. It is not normally a hardware defect. A floating-point number has a fixed number of significant binary digits, and the spacing between representable values grows with magnitude. Whenever an exact result falls between representable values, rounding introduces a small error. Repeated additions accumulate and propagate these errors in ways that depend on their order. Features such as fused multiply-add can also change results by performing a multiplication and addition with only one rounding rather than two.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is a sum of products, such as the sum over k of A[i,k] times B[k,j]. Optimized implementations rarely evaluate these sums strictly from left to right. They divide matrices into tiles, use vector instructions, distribute work among processor cores or GPU threads, and combine partial sums through reduction trees. Different libraries, hardware architectures, thread counts, tile sizes, compiler options, or runtime schedules may therefore combine the same products in different orders.

Because addition is not associative, these different reduction orders can produce slightly different output entries. The differences are often only a few units in the last place, but they may grow when sums are long, values vary greatly in magnitude, or severe cancellation occurs. They can also be amplified by later computations, especially in numerically sensitive algorithms.

Consequently, mathematically equivalent matrix multiplications are not necessarily bitwise reproducible across implementations or execution configurations. Achieving reproducibility requires controlling the reduction order and arithmetic behavior, or using techniques such as higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or reproducible reduction algorithms. These measures generally impose costs in speed, memory use, or parallel scalability, so high-performance libraries often prioritize throughput over identical bit patterns.
